title: Design a Multi-Channel Notification System
prompt: Design a notification system that lets services send messages to users across multiple channels — mobile push, SMS, and email. It must fan out reliably, deduplicate, respect user preferences and rate limits, retry failures, and fall back when a provider is down.
blurb: Multi-channel delivery: fanout, dedup, retries, provider fallback, and rate limiting.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (multi-channel send, preferences, templating, scheduling) from non-functional (reliable delivery, dedup, rate limits, availability).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about channels, volume, delivery guarantees, priority tiers, user preferences/opt-out, provider constraints.

rubric.label: Estimations
rubric.description: Estimates notifications/day, per-channel split, peak fanout (broadcast), queue throughput, provider rate limits.

rubric.label: API design
rubric.description: Send API (single + bulk), notification envelope, template refs, idempotency key, preference/opt-out endpoints.

rubric.label: Data model
rubric.description: Notifications, user channel/contact info, preferences, templates, delivery status log.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Send API → queue → per-channel workers → provider adapters; preference + rate-limit + dedup checks in the path.

rubric.label: Reliability & retries
rubric.description: At-least-once via durable queue, retry with backoff, dead-letter queue, idempotency to avoid duplicate sends.

rubric.label: Deduplication
rubric.description: Idempotency keys, dedup window, avoiding duplicate notifications across retries and multi-producer.

rubric.label: Provider fallback
rubric.description: Multiple providers per channel, health checks, failover, circuit breaking, cost/deliverability routing.

rubric.label: Rate limiting & preferences
rubric.description: Per-user throttling/quiet hours, per-provider rate caps, respecting opt-outs and channel prefs.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Delivery/failure rates by channel/provider, queue lag, retry/DLQ metrics.

functional_requirements: Send notifications via push, SMS, and email
Respect user preferences, opt-outs, and quiet hours
Templating and localization of message content
Bulk/broadcast sends as well as single transactional sends
nonfunctional_requirements: Reliable delivery — at-least-once with dedup (no lost, minimal duplicate)
Respect per-provider and per-user rate limits
Graceful degradation when a provider is down
clarifying_questions: Which channels, and are more expected later?
Volume — notifications/day and peak (e.g. a broadcast to all users)?
Do we own contact info + preferences, or call another service?
qualifying_questions: Are duplicates catastrophic (payment alert) or merely annoying?
Do we need read receipts / delivery confirmation callbacks from providers?

estimations.traffic: 500M notifications/day ≈ ~6K/s avg; a broadcast to 100M users creates a multi-million-item fanout burst
estimations.channels: Split e.g. 60% push / 25% email / 15% SMS; each channel worker pool sized to provider limits
estimations.queues: Durable queue must absorb broadcast bursts (millions enqueued in minutes) and drain within provider rate caps
estimations.storage: Delivery-status log 500M/day × ~200B ≈ ~100GB/day; retain per compliance window

data_model: notifications(notification_id PK, user_id, channel, template_id, payload, priority, idempotency_key, created_at, status)
user_channels(user_id, channel, address, verified) — device tokens, phone, email
delivery_log(notification_id, provider, attempt, status, provider_msg_id, ts)
api_design: POST /notify { user_id | user_ids, template_id, data, channels?, priority, idempotency_key } → { notification_id(s) }
POST /notify/bulk for broadcasts (async, returns job id)
reference.high_level_design: A send request hits the API, which validates and writes the notification with an idempotency key, then enqueues it on a durable queue. Consumers first resolve the target channels against user preferences/opt-outs and quiet hours (dropping or deferring as needed), run a dedup check on the idempotency key, and apply per-user + per-provider rate limits. Surviving notifications route to the appropriate per-channel worker pool, which renders the template and calls a provider adapter. The adapter tries the primary provider; on failure or unhealthy circuit it fails over to a secondary provider. Failures are retried with exponential backoff; exhausted attempts go to a dead-letter queue. Every attempt is recorded in the delivery-status store, updated further by provider delivery callbacks. Broadcasts go through a bulk path that expands the audience into the same queue so all downstream logic (prefs, dedup, rate limits, retries) applies uniformly.

deep_dives.probe: A provider call times out — did it send or not? Walk me through at-least-once delivery with retries and how you avoid double-sending an OTP. What goes to the DLQ and when?
Two services independently trigger the same alert, and retries can re-enqueue. How does the idempotency key work, what's the dedup window, and where do you store dedup state?
Your primary SMS provider degrades. How do you detect it and fail over — health checks, circuit breaker, error-rate thresholds? How do you avoid flapping and duplicate sends during failover?
A provider caps you at 100 msg/s and a user shouldn't get more than 5 pushes/hour. How do you enforce both a per-provider global cap and a per-user cap across many workers?
You broadcast to 100M users. How do you fan that out without overwhelming the queue or the providers, and how do you keep transactional OTPs low-latency during the burst?
You cache user preferences and templates. When a hot template's cache entry expires during a broadcast, how do you avoid a stampede on the preference/template store?

User preferences and contact info live in a database. How do you propagate changes (opt-outs, new device tokens) to the sending pipeline — change data capture with Debezium, or read-through each send? What are the consistency risks of a stale opt-out?

followup_bank.question: How do you guarantee at-least-once without double-sending on an ambiguous provider timeout? What triggers a move to the dead-letter queue?
Where is dedup state stored, what's the dedup window, and how do you dedup across multiple producers and retries?
How do you detect an unhealthy provider and fail over without flapping or duplicate sends — circuit breaker thresholds?
How do you enforce a per-provider global cap AND a per-user cap simultaneously across a distributed worker pool?
For cached preferences/templates, what's the eviction policy and how do you prevent a stampede when a hot entry expires mid-broadcast?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or preferences or store
followup_bank.question: How do you propagate preference/opt-out and device-token changes to the pipeline — CDC/Debezium vs read-through — and what's the risk of a stale opt-out?
How do you keep transactional/high-priority notifications low-latency while a mass broadcast is draining the queue?

scaling: Durable queue absorbs broadcast bursts; per-channel worker pools scale independently
Priority queues/lanes so transactional beats marketing
Per-provider token-bucket rate limiting to respect provider caps
Shard dedup and rate-limit state (Redis) by user/idempotency key
Bulk expansion of broadcasts into the standard pipeline
bottlenecks: Provider rate caps limiting drain rate
Ambiguous provider timeouts causing duplicate risk
Preference/template lookups on the hot path
tradeoffs: At-least-once + dedup (simple, occasional dup risk) vs exactly-once (complex)
Synchronous provider call (immediate status) vs async with callbacks (throughput)
Single provider (simple, risky) vs multi-provider fallback (resilient, complex + cost routing)
Strict per-user rate limits (good UX, may drop) vs deliver-everything
Read-through preferences (fresh) vs cached/CDC (fast, staleness risk on opt-outs)
alternative_solutions: Managed providers with built-in multi-channel (routing all logic to a vendor) vs in-house orchestration
Per-channel dedicated services vs one unified pipeline with channel adapters
Outbox pattern in producer services + CDC to guarantee no lost sends
Priority-partitioned Kafka topics vs a single topic with in-worker prioritization
observability: Delivery success/failure rate by channel and provider
Retry counts and per-provider error rates (feeds circuit breaker)
security: Authn/authz on the send API; scope which services can notify whom
Respect opt-outs and legal consent (SMS/email compliance)
Protect PII (phone/email/device tokens) at rest and in transit
Rate-limit and validate templates to prevent spam/abuse and injection
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer puts a durable queue between the send API and per-channel workers, and threads preference/opt-out checks, idempotency-key dedup, and per-user + per-provider rate limiting into the delivery path. It handles reliability with at-least-once delivery, exponential-backoff retries, a dead-letter queue, and — crucially — reasons about the ambiguous provider timeout so an OTP isn't double-sent (idempotency key + provider message IDs). It routes each channel through provider adapters with health-check/circuit-breaker failover to a secondary provider, and handles broadcasts by expanding them into the same pipeline while protecting transactional traffic with priority lanes. It proactively raises provider rate caps, broadcast-vs-transactional starvation, and duplicate risk as the main challenges, and addresses propagating preference/opt-out changes (CDC vs read-through) and cache stampede on hot templates/preferences.

interviewer_notes: This is mid-level, so reliability and dedup are the decisive dimensions. Push the ambiguous-timeout scenario hard: 'the provider call timed out — did it send?' — a strong candidate reaches idempotency keys and at-least-once with dedup rather than hand-waving. Make them enforce two rate limits at once (per-provider global + per-user) across distributed workers. Provider fallback with a circuit breaker is good senior-leaning signal. If they store preferences in a database, fire the CDC/Debezium probe (stale opt-out risk); if they cache templates/preferences, fire the eviction/stampede probe. The broadcast-vs-transactional priority question is a good closer.
